questions.title: How does backpropagating through a frozen, 4-bit quantized model without updating those weights actually work mathematically?
questions.question_body: I am reading the QLoRA paper and I understand the core idea: we keep the base model weights ($\mathbf{W}^{{\text{NF4}}}$) frozen and only tune the adapters ($\mathbf{L}_1, \mathbf{L}_2$). However, I am struggling with the mechanics of backpropagation. The paper states 'backpropagates gradients through a frozen... model into Low Rank Adapters.' If $\mathbf{W}$ is frozen, shouldn't the gradient with respect to it be zero or NaN? Specifically, when calculating $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{L}_i}$, how do we compute the term involving $\frac{\partial \mathbf{X}}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$ if $\mathbf{W}$ is stored in NF4 format and never updated? Is it simply that we compute numerical gradients locally around the dequantized value without performing any weight update step on $\mathbf{W}$, or is there a specific chain rule derivation I'm missing regarding the dequantization function in Equation (5)?

questions.title: What is the specific mechanism by which Double Quantization achieves 'information theoretically optimal' savings without losing precision?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 (QLoRA Finetuning), the authors introduce Double Quantization (DQ) to save memory. They claim it reduces memory by ~0.37 bits/parameter by quantizing the quantization constants ($c_2$). The text mentions: 'treatment of quantization constants $c_2^{${\text{FP32}}}$... as inputs to a second quantization.' I am confused about the implementation details here. Are $c_2$ values converted from FP32 to FP8 for storage, and then when needed during dequantization (Equation 6), do we perform a second dequantization step on-the-fly to recover an approximate FP32 constant before applying it to the NF4 weights? If DQ is only used for storage but not for forward/backward computation except via approximation, how exactly does this mapping ensure that no significant precision is lost compared to storing full FP32 constants? Is there a lossless recovery guaranteed, or just sufficient accuracy for training stability?

questions.title: Does Paged Optimizers solve Memory Spikes or just Out-of-Memory (OOM) crashes during long sequence generation?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to understand the specific utility of 'Paged Optimizers' mentioned in Section 4 and discussed in Section 5. The paper states they are used 'to prevent memory spikes during gradient checkpointing that occur when processing a mini-batch with a long sequence length.' My understanding of gradient checkpointing usually involves trading compute for memory by recomputing activations. However, I am confused about where exactly these 'spikes' occur in LoRA finetuning compared to full finetuning. If LoRA parameters are tiny by design (0.2% of base model), why does their optimizers state cause such significant GPU memory issues compared to the four-bit base model weights? Does 'Paged Optimizers' essentially mean redistributing optimizer states between CPU RAM and GPU VRAM dynamically based on which parameters are currently being updated in a given batch, effectively making them an offloading solution specifically for optimizer states rather than activation gradients?

questions.title: Why was NF4 chosen as information-theoretically optimal if Quantile Quantization already ensures equal bin occupancy?
questions.question_body: In Section 4, regarding 4-bit NormalFloat Quantization, the authors explain that NF4 addresses limitations of standard Quantile Quantization. They state that Quantile estimation is expensive and approximation errors affect outliers. They then propose transforming weights so they fit into a fixed range $[-1,1]$ matching the data type's distribution. However, I am still unclear on why this makes it 'optimal.' Quantile Quantization defines bins such that each bin has exactly $1/2^k$ probability mass under a theoretical distribution. How does fixing standard deviation $\sigma$ to fit $[-1,1]$ specifically improve upon just estimating quantiles directly from data? Is it because precomputing these bins avoids runtime cost entirely, making it more stable for training where distributions shift slightly batch-to-batch due to gradient updates? In what specific mathematical way does mapping data to $N(0,S)$ with pre-defined bins minimize reconstruction error compared to dynamic bin estimation?

questions.title: '0% iterations' despite using 0.2% LoRA parameters: Why did setting adapters at *every* layer become crucial after non-linearities in large models?
questions.question_body:
The authors mention they use adapters at every network layer ('adapter at every linear transformer block layer'). Standard LoRA papers often applied them only to Query and Value projections in_attention blocks._para

I read somewhere else that applying adapters only at certain layers or even across all layers might have diminishing returns due to computational cost. But here, applying them everywhere seems necessary.

The text says: "...avoid[s] almost all of the accuracy tradeoffs seen in prior work." Could someone explain *why* using adapters at every intermediate FFN block (and potentially Input/Output layers as well) became so critical for recovering full 16-bit performance compared to earlier applications?

In LLaMA architecture there are residual connections after non-linearity
